title: What everything is made of: particles and atoms
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 4 Chemistry: Unit 3.1 'Materials, substances and particles' (matter, materials and substances; the particle model of solids, liquids and gases; particles always moving). Adds the history of the atom idea (Kanada and Democritus), evidence for particles (Brownian motion), density, and the empty space inside atoms. No textbook needed.
summary: Everything around you, even air, is made of particles far too small to see. Your child finds out that matter is anything that has mass and takes up space, so air counts but light and shadows don't. They act out how particles are arranged and move in solids, liquids and gases, watch colour spread in still water, and model the jiggling that Robert Brown saw and Einstein explained. They float and sink things to discover density, and see where sugar goes when it dissolves. Then they learn that an atom is almost all empty space, and that what we feel as touching is electric pushing. Along the way they meet Kanada and Democritus, who first imagined atoms, and the scientists who proved atoms are real.
builds_on: Materials (Classes 1–3): objects and materials, properties, natural and made, transparent to opaque, solids, liquids and gases sorted by whether they flow. Changing materials (Class 2): melting, burning and 'nothing disappears'. Changing materials (Class 4) uses this rung's particle model to explain melting, expansion and reactions. Next: Gases, evaporation, condensation and solutions (Class 5) uses particles to explain evaporation, condensation, gas pressure and dissolving.
subconcepts: matter: anything that has mass and takes up space
the particle model: everything is made of tiny particles
particles in solids, liquids and gases: how they are arranged and how they move
particles are always moving, faster when hotter: diffusion
Brownian motion: evidence for invisible particles
mass, volume and density: why things float or sink
air has mass and takes up space
spaces between particles: dissolving and mixing
crystals: particles in a repeating order
the atom is mostly empty space; 'touching' is electric pushing
old ideas of atoms: Kanada's paramanu and Democritus's atomos
goals: By the end your child can explain what matter is, and argue whether air, light, smell and shadows are matter.
By the end your child can describe and act out the arrangement and movement of particles in solids, liquids and gases.
By the end your child can explain diffusion and why it is faster in hot water.
By the end your child can explain what Brown saw and why it is evidence for particles.
By the end your child can predict float or sink using the idea of density, and test it.
By the end your child can explain that atoms are mostly empty space, and tell the stories of Kanada, Democritus and the scientists who proved atoms real.
words: matter
anything that has mass and takes up space
mass
how much stuff something has, measured in grams and kilograms
volume
how much space something takes up, measured in millilitres or cubic centimetres
density
how much mass is packed into a space; dense things sink in less dense liquids
particle
a tiny piece of matter, far too small to see
atom
the smallest piece of an element; there are about 90 kinds found in nature
element
a substance made of only one kind of atom, like oxygen, carbon, iron or gold
molecule
two or more atoms joined together, like water (two hydrogens and one oxygen)
substance
one pure kind of matter, like water, salt or iron
diffusion
particles spreading out from where there are many to where there are few
Brownian motion
the jiggling of tiny specks pushed about by invisible particles hitting them
nucleus
the tiny, heavy centre of an atom

days.title: Is it matter?
days.goal: Recall materials and decide what counts as matter.

steps.title: From materials to matter
steps.do: Remember last year's lessons on materials. Ask: 'What are the three states of matter?' (Solid, liquid and gas.) 'Last year you pushed an upside-down glass with a tissue inside it into a bucket of water. Why did the tissue stay dry?' (The glass was full of air, and air takes up space.) Say: 'This year we ask what all materials are made of, deep down.'

steps.title: Does air weigh anything?
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Hang a ruler from its middle by a thread, with an equally blown-up balloon taped to each end, so it balances. Ask: 'If I let the air out of one balloon, what will happen? Why?' Then a grown-up puts a piece of tape on one balloon near the knot and pricks it through the tape with a pin, so the air leaks out slowly. The side with the full balloon drops. Say: 'The full balloon holds squeezed air, which is heavier than the same space of ordinary air. So air has mass. Air is matter: it has mass and takes up space.' Ask: 'How much do you think the air in this room weighs?' (A room 4 metres long, 4 metres wide and 3 metres high holds about 58 kg of air, about as much as a grown-up.)

steps.title: Is It Matter? cards
steps.do: Play the card game g1. Each card names something: a stone, air, a rainbow, a smell, a thought, a shadow, fire, music. Teams sort them into MATTER, NOT MATTER, or ARGUE IT, and must give a reason using the test 'Does it have mass? Does it take up space?' Let your child argue the hard ones (fire is hot glowing gases, which are matter, giving out light, which isn't; a smell is particles reaching your nose; a thought happens in a brain made of matter, but is the thought itself matter? Nobody can say for sure).

steps.title: Material, substance, mixture
steps.do: Hold up a glass of water, a spoon of salt, a steel spoon and a tumbler of rasam. Say: 'Pure water is a substance: one pure kind of matter. Salt is a substance too. Steel is a material, but it is a mixture of iron, carbon and a few other things. Rasam is a mixture of many substances.' Ask your child to name three substances and three mixtures in the kitchen. (Substances: water, sugar, salt, baking soda. Mixtures: dal, milk, air, atta, soil.)

need: 2 balloons, a ruler or stick, thread, a pin and tape (grown-up)
the printed Is It Matter? cards
a glass of water, salt, a steel spoon, a tumbler of rasam

days.title: How small can you cut?
days.goal: Follow the 2,500-year-old thought experiment that led to the idea of atoms.

steps.title: Cut it in half
steps.do: Give your child a long strip of paper (an A4 sheet cut lengthways). They cut it in half, then cut one half in half, and so on, counting the cuts, until the scissors can't cut any more (usually 7 to 9 cuts). Ask: 'If you had perfect scissors and perfect eyes, could you go on for ever? Or would you reach a piece that cannot be cut?' Let them argue both sides. Say: 'Two thinkers asked this question more than 2,000 years ago, in two different countries.'

steps.title: Kanada and Democritus
steps.do: Tell voice v1. Kanada, a thinker in ancient India, taught that everything is made of tiny particles called paramanu, which join in twos and threes to make bigger things. Democritus, in ancient Greece, taught that everything is made of atoms moving in empty space. Atomos is Greek for 'uncuttable'. Ask: 'Neither of them had a microscope. How do you think they decided?' (By thinking and arguing, not by experiments.) Ask the voice's question. Then say: 'Today we know atoms are real, but they can be split into even smaller parts. So Kanada and Democritus were right that tiny particles exist, and wrong that they can never be cut.'

steps.title: Dot painting
steps.do: Your child makes a picture using only dots, with a cotton bud dipped in paint or with felt-pen dots, and no lines at all: a mango, a face or a tree. Then stand back two metres. Ask: 'Up close, what do you see? From far away?' (Dots. A picture.) Say: 'The painter Georges Seurat painted like this, in dots. Your phone screen is made of tiny dots called pixels.' Look at a phone screen with a magnifying glass to see the pixels. Say: 'Matter is a bit like this: it is made of particles far too small to see.'

need: paints and cotton buds or felt pens, paper
a magnifying glass and a phone

days.title: Be the particles
days.goal: Learn the particle model by dancing, acting and making music.

steps.title: The particle dance
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Use as many family members as you can, or your child plus toys as fellow particles. SOLID: stand close together in neat rows, arms linked, vibrating on the spot but never moving away. LIQUID: unlink arms but stay close, sliding past each other, keeping in a group that fills the bottom of the room. GAS: spread out and move fast in straight lines, bouncing off the walls and each other, filling the whole room. Now heat them (call 'HEAT!'): solid particles vibrate harder until they break free and become liquid; liquid particles speed up until they fly off as gas. Then 'COOL!' and reverse. Ask: 'When we melted, did we become different particles?' (no, the same particles, moving differently).

steps.title: Draw the model
steps.do: Your child draws three boxes and draws particles as circles: SOLID (circles touching in neat rows), LIQUID (circles touching but jumbled), GAS (a few circles far apart with movement arrows). Ask: 'Why can you pour a liquid but not a solid?' (liquid particles can slide past each other). 'Why can you squash a gas but not a liquid?' (gas particles have big spaces between them). Test with a syringe: block the end with a finger and push. Air squashes; water barely does.

steps.title: The music of matter
steps.do: Make three pieces of music with spoons, a steel plate, a glass and your voices. Solid: a steady, regular beat that never changes, everyone together (tap, tap, tap). Liquid: a flowing tune that slides up and down, notes running into each other. Gas: random pops, clicks and whooshes from everywhere, fast and scattered. Record them if you can. Ask: 'Which music had the most order? Which had the most freedom? Which state of matter does each one match, and why?'

steps.title: Build molecules
steps.do: Your child rolls small balls of atta dough or clay: big balls for oxygen atoms and small balls for hydrogen atoms. Join them with toothpicks. Make a water molecule: one oxygen in the middle, joined to two hydrogens. Then make an oxygen molecule: two oxygen atoms joined together. Say: 'Atoms join together to make molecules. A water molecule is made of three atoms.' Ask: 'Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, which are both gases. Is water like either of them?' (No. Joined atoms make a new substance with new properties.)

need: space to move, atta dough or clay, toothpicks
spoons, a steel plate, a glass

days.title: Particles never stop
days.goal: See particles spread on their own, faster when hot, and meet the story.

steps.title: Hot and cold colour drop
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Fill one glass with cold water from the fridge, and a grown-up fills another with hot water from a kettle or geyser, about as hot as tea. Wait one minute so the water is still. Ask: 'Will the colour spread if nobody stirs? Which glass will be faster?' Your child adds one drop of food colour to each at the same time, without stirring. Watch for 5 minutes. Ask: 'Which spread faster? Nobody stirred it. What moved the colour?' (The water particles are always moving and bump the colour particles about. In hot water the particles move faster.)

steps.title: The smell race
steps.do: Your child stands at the far end of a room with eyes closed, and raises a hand the moment they smell something. A grown-up at the other end opens a jar of crushed elaichi (cardamom) and starts a timer. Ask: 'How did the smell cross the room?' (Smell particles spread out through the air. Air particles jostle them along, and small air currents carry them too.) Say: 'Particles spreading out on their own, from where there are many to where there are few, is called diffusion.'

steps.title: Story: The Dance No One Could See
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain. Ask: 'What did Robert Brown think made the specks dance at first?' (that they were alive). 'Why did he change his mind?' (dust from rocks and glass danced too). 'What was really moving them?' (invisible water particles bumping into them from every side).

steps.title: Were atoms real?
steps.do: Tell voice v2, the long argument about whether atoms are real, and how Einstein and Perrin finally settled it using the jiggling Brown saw. Ask the voice's question. Then ask: 'Can we be sure something exists if we can't see it? What else do we know about without seeing it?' (Air, wind, gravity, germs, other people's feelings.)

need: two clear glasses, cold water and hot water (grown-up)

days.title: The hidden crowd
days.goal: Model Brownian motion and check understanding of the particle model.

steps.title: The hidden crowd model
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Pour a thin layer of dry rice into a shoebox lid or a tray with sides. Put a ping-pong ball (or a small paper ball) on top. Your child shakes the tray gently, in small random jerks, without tilting it. Watch only the ball: it jiggles about with no pattern, like Brown's specks. Now ask a family member who didn't see the set-up to crouch with their eyes level with the rim, so they can see the top of the ball but not the rice. Ask them: 'Why is the ball moving?' Say: 'They can't see the rice grains, only the ball. Brown couldn't see the water particles, only the specks. The jiggling is the evidence.' Ask: 'Would a bigger ball jiggle more or less?' (Less. More grains hit it from every side, and their pushes even out. That is why big things don't jiggle.)

steps.title: Dust in a sunbeam
steps.do: Darken a room except for one sunbeam through a gap in the curtains, or shine a torch in a dark room. Shake a dusty cloth once near the beam and watch the specks drift and swirl. Ask: 'Is this the jiggling Brown saw?' Then say: 'Mostly not. Most of this swirling comes from gentle air currents in the room. Real Brownian motion needs a microscope. The Roman poet Lucretius thought dust in a sunbeam showed atoms at work. He was right that atoms exist, but this swirling is mostly moving air.'

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. For the written items, ask your child to use the words particle, arrangement and movement.

steps.title: Never still
steps.do: Ask your child to sit completely still for one minute, eyes closed, breathing slowly. Then ask: 'Were you completely still?' Talk about it: your heart beat, blood flowed, air moved in and out, and every particle of your body kept vibrating. Ask: 'Is anything in the universe ever perfectly still?' Scientists say no. Particles slow down as things get colder, but even at the coldest possible temperature, minus 273 °C, they would still jiggle a tiny bit. And that temperature can never quite be reached.

need: a shoebox lid or tray with sides, a cup of dry rice, a ping-pong ball or paper ball
a sunbeam or a torch, a dusty cloth

days.title: Float or sink: density
days.goal: Discover that floating depends on how tightly mass is packed, not on size.

steps.title: Float or sink: weigh, predict, test
steps.do: Do Experiment e3, the float-or-sink table. Collect 10 objects: a wooden belan (rolling pin), a steel coin, a candle, a potato, an apple, a plastic bottle cap, a lemon, an ice cube, a big steel spoon and a lump of clay or plasticine. Your child weighs each on a kitchen scale and writes the mass in grams. (No scale? Put them in order from heaviest to lightest by holding them in your hands.) For each one, they guess float or sink, then test it in a bucket of water. Ask: 'Is it the heaviest things that sink?' (No. The heavy belan floats and the light coin sinks.) Then roll the clay into a ball and test it: it sinks. Shape the same clay into a boat with thin walls and test again: it floats. Ask: 'Same clay, same mass. What changed?' (The boat takes up more space, because it holds air inside, so the boat as a whole is less dense than water.)

steps.title: The floating egg
steps.do: Put a raw egg in a glass of tap water: the egg sinks. Ask: 'What could we add to the water to make the egg float?' Take the egg out and stir in one big spoon of salt at a time, testing the egg after each spoon, until the egg floats (usually after 4 to 6 spoons). Ask: 'Did the egg change?' (No. The salt added mass to the water, but the water took up hardly any more space, so the salty water is denser.) Then pour a spoon of cooking oil onto water: it floats on top. Ask: 'Which is denser, oil or water?' (Water.) Ice floats too, because water expands when it freezes, so ice is less dense than water.

steps.title: What is density?
steps.do: Explain with a picture: draw two boxes of the same size. In one, draw 5 particles. In the other, draw 20 particles packed tight. Say: 'Density is how much mass is packed into a space. If something is denser than water, it sinks. If it is less dense, it floats.' Ask: 'A huge steel ship floats. How?' (Its steel is shaped around a big space full of air, so the whole ship, steel plus air, is less dense than water.) Ask: 'Why is it easier to float in the sea than in a river?' (Sea water is salty, so it is denser than river water and pushes up more strongly.)

need: a kitchen scale, if you have one
a raw egg, salt, a tall glass, cooking oil

days.title: Dissolving, and crystals
days.goal: See where dissolved sugar goes, and start growing crystals.

steps.title: Where does the sugar go?
steps.do: Do Experiment e4. Fill a clear glass to the very brim with water. Ask: 'Can I add a spoon of sugar without it spilling?' Sprinkle in one level teaspoon of sugar slowly and watch the crystals disappear. Repeat, counting the spoons, until water spills. Your child tastes a drop on a clean spoon. Ask: 'Where did the sugar go?' (It broke up into particles too small to see, spread out among the water particles. The sweet taste shows it is still there.) Then measure one cup of whole chana and one cup of rava (sooji), mix them, and pour the mixture back into the measuring cup. Ask first: 'Will one cup and one cup make two cups?' (No. The small rava grains slip into the gaps between the chana.) Say: 'Small particles can fit into gaps between bigger ones. When salt dissolves in water, the mixture takes up a little less space than the salt and water did apart, because the particles pack closely together.'

steps.title: Start a crystal garden
steps.do: Start the project. A grown-up heats a cup of water until it is about as hot as tea. Your child stirs in phitkari (alum) powder, one spoon at a time, until no more dissolves. (Salt also works, but grows crystals more slowly.) Pour the clear liquid into a clean glass jar. Tie a cotton thread to a pencil, lay the pencil across the top, and let the thread hang into the liquid, with a paper clip at the end as a weight. Put the jar where nobody will move it. Each day, look at the thread: crystals grow on it as the liquid cools and slowly dries up. Now look at grains of salt with a magnifying glass: they are tiny cubes. Say: 'In a crystal, particles line up in the same pattern again and again, like tiles on a floor. That is why salt crystals are cubes.'

steps.title: Tile a crystal
steps.do: Your child cuts 30 small squares of coloured paper and sticks them on a sheet in a pattern that repeats exactly: this is like a crystal. Then they make a second picture with the same squares jumbled: this is like glass, a solid whose particles have no repeating order. Ask: 'Which picture is like a grain of salt? Which is like a glass bangle?' Then tell this: in 1982 a scientist, Dan Shechtman, found a crystal whose pattern is ordered but never quite repeats. Most scientists said this was impossible, and he was mocked for years. He won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2011.

need: a glass, water, sugar, a teaspoon
1 cup whole chana and 1 cup rava (sooji), a measuring cup
phitkari (alum) or salt, a glass jar, cotton thread, a pencil and a paper clip

days.title: The emptiness inside
days.goal: Discover that atoms are mostly empty space and that touching is electric pushing.

steps.title: The bullets that bounced back
steps.do: Tell voice v3. In 1909, in Manchester, Hans Geiger and a 20-year-old student, Ernest Marsden, fired tiny particles called alpha particles at gold foil much thinner than a page. Almost all went straight through, as if nothing was there. But about one in every 8,000 bounced back. Ask: 'If most particles pass straight through, what do you think an atom is like inside?' Their professor, Ernest Rutherford, said it was as if you fired a cannon shell at tissue paper and it came back and hit you. Ask the voice's question.

steps.title: The pea in the stadium
steps.do: Go to the biggest open space you can reach: a park, a maidan, a school ground or your building's compound. (If you can't go out, look at a cricket stadium on a map or on TV.) Put a pea (or a peppercorn) in the very middle. Say: 'If an atom were as big as this whole ground, its nucleus would be this pea in the middle. The electrons would be a faint blur spread through the whole space. Everything else is empty.' Walk from the pea to the edge counting steps. Ask: 'If atoms are almost all empty, why can't I walk through a wall?'

steps.title: Pushing without touching
steps.do: Do Experiment e5. First ask: 'Can two things push each other without touching?' Rub two balloons on your hair or a woollen sweater and hang them side by side on threads: they push apart without touching. Then bring a rubbed balloon near small bits of paper: they jump up to it. Say: 'Electric forces push and pull without touching. When your hand presses a table, the electrons in your hand and the electrons in the table push each other away, very strongly. That push is what you feel as touching, and it is what makes the table feel solid.' Ask: 'So is the table solid or empty?' (Both: it is mostly empty space, but the electric push makes it feel solid.)

steps.title: Particles from space
steps.do: Tell voice v4, Bibha Chowdhuri, who recorded the tracks of particles from space on photographic plates in the mountains near Darjeeling. Say: 'Right now, tiny particles from space called muons are passing through your body, many every second.' Ask the voice's question.

need: 2 balloons, thread, a woollen sweater, bits of paper

days.title: Crystals, posters and teach it back
days.goal: Finish the project, play with harder ideas and explain the whole rung.

steps.title: The crystal garden and particle poster
steps.do: Finish the project. Look at the crystal thread with a magnifier and draw the crystal shapes. Then your child makes a poster called 'What everything is made of': the three states in particles, a diffusion picture, Brown's jiggling speck, the float-or-sink table, and the pea in the stadium. Ask: 'Which idea surprised you most?'

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2. Use the float-or-sink table from Day 6 for the density questions.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3, sections A and B. The written questions are big; let your child talk first and then write the best sentence.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches a family member, using the poster: what matter is, the particle model (with a quick particle dance), diffusion, Brown's dancing specks, density, and the empty atom. They finish by telling the story of Kanada and Democritus in one minute. Then ask the check questions.

need: a large sheet of paper and pens

experiments.title: Does air weigh anything?
experiments.question: Does air have mass?
need: 2 balloons blown up to the same size
steps: Tie a thread to the middle of the stick and hang it from a hook or a chair back.
Tape one balloon to each end. Slide them until the stick balances level.
Put a small piece of tape on one balloon near the knot.
A grown-up pricks the balloon through the tape so the air leaks out slowly.
Watch the stick.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will happen to the balance when one balloon empties?'
experiments.observe: The side with the full balloon goes down.
experiments.why: The full balloon holds squeezed air, which is denser than the air around it, so that side has a little extra mass that pulls it down. Air is made of particles (mostly nitrogen and oxygen molecules) and has mass, about 1.2 grams for every litre at room temperature. Air is matter.
experiments.safety: A grown-up handles the pin. Balloon pieces are a choking risk for small children; pick them all up.

experiments.title: Hot and cold colour drop
experiments.question: Do particles move on their own, and faster when hot?
need: hot water from a kettle or geyser (a grown-up)
steps: Fill one glass with cold water and one with hot water.
Wait one minute until the water is still.
Add one drop of food colour to each at the same moment. Do not stir.
Watch for 5 minutes and draw what you see at 1, 3 and 5 minutes.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the colour spread without stirring? Which glass will spread faster?'
experiments.observe: The colour spreads in both, without stirring, but much faster in the hot water.
experiments.why: Water particles are always moving and bumping into the colour particles, spreading them out from where there are many to where there are few: diffusion. In hot water the particles move faster, so diffusion is faster. Some of the spreading in the hot glass is also from currents of warm water rising.
experiments.safety: A grown-up handles the hot water.

experiments.title: Float or sink: weigh, predict, test
experiments.question: Do heavy things always sink?
need: a kitchen scale, if you have one
10 objects: a wooden belan, a steel coin, a candle, a potato, an apple, a bottle cap, a lemon, an ice cube, a big steel spoon, a lump of clay
steps: Weigh each object and write its mass.
Write your guess: float or sink.
Test each one gently in the bucket.
Roll the clay into a ball and test; then shape the same clay into a boat and test again.
Look for a pattern.
experiments.predict: Your child predicts before each test, and also predicts: 'Will the heaviest things sink?'
experiments.observe: Floating doesn't match mass: the heavy wooden belan floats, and the light coin sinks. The clay ball sinks but the clay boat floats.
experiments.why: Whether something floats depends on its density (mass for its volume) compared with water's. Wood, wax, apples and ice are less dense than water, so they float; steel, stone and clay balls are denser, so they sink. Shaping clay into a boat makes it enclose air, so the boat as a whole is less dense than water. Water also pushes up on anything in it (upthrust).
experiments.safety: Mop up spills; supervise children near buckets of water.

experiments.title: Where does the sugar go?
experiments.question: When sugar dissolves, where does it go?
need: a clear glass filled to the brim with water
one cup of whole chana and one cup of rava (sooji)
steps: Fill the glass to the very brim.
Sprinkle in one level teaspoon of sugar slowly and let it dissolve. Repeat, counting.
Stop when water spills. Taste a drop on a clean spoon.
Mix exactly one cup of whole chana with one cup of rava and measure the mixture.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Can sugar go in without a spill? Where will the sugar go? Will one cup plus one cup make two cups?'
experiments.observe: The first spoons go in without a spill: the sugar crystals disappear, and the water surface bulges a little above the rim. The water tastes sweet. The chana-and-rava mixture is clearly less than two cups.
experiments.why: The sugar has not vanished. It has broken up into particles far too small to see, spread out among the water particles, as the sweet taste shows. A spoonful of sugar is partly air between the grains, and water can bulge a little above the rim before it spills, so a few spoons fit. The chana and rava show something else that is true of particles: small ones can fit into the gaps between big ones. When salt dissolves in water, the mixture takes up a little less space than the salt and water did apart, because the particles pack closely together.
experiments.safety: Use a clean spoon for tasting.

experiments.title: Pushing without touching
experiments.question: Can things push each other without touching?
steps: Blow up and tie the balloons; tie a thread to each.
Rub both balloons on hair or wool.
Hold them up by their threads side by side.
Bring one rubbed balloon near the bits of tissue.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will the two rubbed balloons do when they hang together?'
experiments.observe: The rubbed balloons push apart without touching. The tissue bits jump up to the balloon.
experiments.why: Rubbing moves tiny particles called electrons onto the balloons, giving them the same electric charge, and same charges push each other away, across empty space. The atoms in your hand and in a table also push each other away through their electrons, very strongly, long before their nuclei come anywhere near each other. That push is the 'solidness' we feel.
experiments.safety: Balloon pieces are a choking risk for small children.

activities.title: The particle dance
steps: Solid: close rows, linked arms, vibrate on the spot.
Liquid: close but free, slide past each other.
Gas: far apart, fast, bounce off walls.
Call HEAT and COOL to change state.
Ask whether the particles changed or only their movement.
activities.outcome: A felt, physical model of the three states and changes of state.

activities.title: The hidden crowd
need: a shoebox lid or a tray with sides
a ping-pong ball or paper ball
steps: Spread rice in the tray and put the ball on top.
Shake the tray in small random jerks.
Watch only the ball.
A family member crouches with eyes level with the rim, sees only the top of the ball, and guesses why it moves.
Try a bigger ball.
activities.outcome: A model of Brownian motion: the visible jiggle is evidence for an invisible crowd.

project.title: Crystal garden and 'What everything is made of' poster
steps: With a grown-up's help, dissolve as much phitkari (alum) or salt as will dissolve in a cup of hot water.
Hang a thread in it and leave it somewhere still.
Look each day and draw the crystals.
Make a poster: the three states in particles, diffusion, Brown's specks, density, the empty atom, the crystal.
Present the poster to the family.
project.outcome: Real crystals grown at home and a poster that tells the whole story of matter.

game.title: Is It Matter?
need: three sheets labelled MATTER, NOT MATTER, ARGUE IT
rules: Cut out the cards and shuffle them face down. The back of each card has the scientists' usual answer.
Teams take turns to draw a card and read it aloud.
The team decides MATTER, NOT MATTER or ARGUE IT, and must give a reason using the test: 'Does it have mass? Does it take up space?'
Turn the card over. A matching answer with a good reason wins the card.
For ARGUE IT cards, each team gives its best argument, and the other team decides which argument was better.
The team with most cards wins.

big: If atoms are almost all empty, why does anything feel solid? What does 'solid' really mean?
If the atoms in your body were once in stars, rocks, rivers and other living things, where does 'you' begin and end?
Can we know something exists if we can never see it?
Is a thought made of matter? Is love?
Kanada and Democritus reached the same idea far apart. Do ideas belong to one people, or to everyone?

challenge.q: Some say Kanada discovered the atom two thousand years before Western scientists. Is that right?
challenge.hint: Kanada really did teach that matter is made of tiny eternal particles (paramanu) that combine, in the Vaisheshika school. But his dates are uncertain (scholars suggest anywhere from about the 6th to the 2nd century BCE), Democritus in Greece had a similar idea around the same era, and neither was based on experiments. John Dalton (1808) gave chemical evidence, and atoms were only proved real around 1905–1908. Ask: what's the difference between a brilliant guess and a discovery? Can a guess still deserve credit?

challenge.q: We draw atoms as tiny solar systems, with electrons circling like planets. Is that what they look like?
challenge.hint: Not really. That picture (from Niels Bohr, 1913) was a useful step, but electrons don't have neat orbits; they are better described as fuzzy clouds where an electron is likely to be found. Ask: why do we keep using pictures we know are not quite right?

challenge.q: Dust dancing in a sunbeam shows atoms bumping it. True?
challenge.hint: Mostly no. The dust you can see swirls in tiny air currents. True Brownian motion is visible only for much smaller specks, under a microscope. The Roman poet Lucretius used the sunbeam as his example; the idea was right, the example was mostly wrong. Ask: can a wrong example lead to a right idea?

perspectives.view: It sorted reality into categories (substance, quality, action and more) and taught that visible things are built from invisible paramanu combining in pairs and triads. Ask: why might ancient thinkers in India and Greece have reached a similar idea? Did they ever hear of each other?

Many physicists describe particles as ripples or excitations in invisible fields that fill all space, more like notes played on an instrument than like tiny balls. This is one way of describing what the mathematics says. Ask: if particles are like notes, what is the instrument?

A grain of salt is a crystal made of particles of sodium and chlorine, arranged in a cube pattern. Ask: how many particles do you think are in one grain? (About a billion billion: 1 followed by 18 zeros.)

voices.who: Kanada (Vaisheshika school, ancient India; dates uncertain, perhaps between the 6th and 2nd centuries BCE) and Democritus (Greece, about 460–370 BCE)
voices.idea: Kanada taught that all physical things are made of paramanu: tiny, eternal, indivisible particles of earth, water, fire and air, which combine in pairs (dvyanuka) and triads (tryanuka) to form larger things. Democritus, following his teacher Leucippus, said everything is made of atomos ('uncuttable') particles moving through empty space, differing in shape and size.
voices.then: Both were philosophers, not experimenters. In Greece, Aristotle rejected atoms and his view dominated Europe for nearly 2,000 years; in India, other schools of thought argued with the Vaisheshika view.
voices.now: Atoms are real, but they are not uncuttable: they are made of protons, neutrons and electrons, and protons and neutrons are made of quarks. Historians agree both traditions independently imagined matter made of tiny particles. Who was first is uncertain, because Kanada's dates are not known; claims that he was clearly earlier than Democritus go beyond the evidence.
voices.ask: Kanada and Democritus guessed something true without experiments. What do you need to turn a good guess into knowledge?

voices.who: Ludwig Boltzmann (1844–1906), Austria; Albert Einstein (1879–1955); Jean Perrin (1870–1942), France
voices.idea: Boltzmann explained heat, temperature and gas pressure as the result of countless tiny particles moving at random. In 1905, Einstein, then working in a patent office, showed mathematically that Brown's jiggling specks were being pushed by invisible molecules, and predicted how far they should wander. In 1908 Perrin measured it carefully and found Einstein was right.
voices.then: Powerful scientists, including Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald, argued that atoms were only a useful idea, not real things. Boltzmann spent years defending atoms and suffered deeply from the attacks; he died in 1906, before the question was settled.
voices.now: Perrin's measurements convinced almost everyone, including Ostwald, that atoms are real. Perrin won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1926. Today we can even make pictures of single atoms with special microscopes.
voices.ask: Boltzmann was right, but most people didn't believe him while he was alive. How should scientists treat an idea that most of them think is wrong?

voices.who: Hans Geiger (1882–1945), Ernest Marsden (1889–1970) and Ernest Rutherford (1871–1937), Manchester, England
voices.idea: In 1909, Geiger and Marsden, then a 20-year-old student, fired alpha particles at very thin gold foil and counted, in a dark room, the tiny flashes they made on a screen. Almost all went straight through, but about one in 8,000 bounced back sharply. In 1911 Rutherford explained this: an atom has a tiny, heavy, positively charged nucleus, and the rest is almost entirely empty space.
voices.then: Scientists had pictured atoms as solid 'plum puddings' of charge (J.J. Thomson's model). The result was so surprising that Rutherford said it was like firing a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and having it come back and hit you.
voices.now: The nuclear atom is accepted. The model is usually named after Rutherford; Geiger is remembered for his counter; Marsden, who did much of the patient counting, is far less known.
voices.ask: The student counted flashes in the dark for hours; the professor explained them. Who discovered the nucleus?

voices.who: Bibha Chowdhuri (1913–1991) and D.M. Bose (1885–1975), Bose Institute, Calcutta
voices.idea: Between 1939 and 1942, Chowdhuri and Bose exposed photographic plates to cosmic rays (particles raining down from space) on mountains near Darjeeling. In their plates they found tracks of particles they called mesons, and published their results in the journal Nature in 1941 and 1942, estimating the particles' mass.
voices.then: During the Second World War, they could not get the newer, more sensitive photographic plates from Europe, so their tracks were faint. In 1947, Cecil Powell's team in Bristol, using better plates (building on a method pioneered by the Austrian physicist Marietta Blau), discovered the pion. Powell won the 1950 Nobel Prize.
voices.now: Historians now recognise Chowdhuri and Bose's work as an important early step, and Powell himself noted it. Chowdhuri was largely forgotten for decades; in 2019 a star was named after her (HD 86081, renamed 'Bibha').
voices.ask: They had the right idea but not the best equipment because of a war. Is it fair that the team with better plates got the prize? What would be fairer?

story.title: The Dance No One Could See
text: I am a speck. I am so small that a thousand of me, lined up, would not reach across the head of a pin. I lived inside a grain of pollen, the yellow dust that flowers make, from a pink wild flower called Clarkia, in the summer of 1827.

The botanist's name was Robert Brown. He was a quiet Scottish man who had sailed to Australia and come back with thousands of dried plants, and who now spent his days bent over a microscope with a single small lens, looking at the insides of flowers.

One June morning he tipped some pollen grains into a drop of water on a strip of glass, and the grains, soaking up the water, burst open, and out we came: hundreds of specks like me, tumbling into the water.
And we danced.

I don't know how else to say it. I did not decide to move. I did not want to move. But I moved: a little to the left, a jerk upwards, a shiver, a skip to the right, never still for a moment, never in a straight line. All around me, my brothers and sisters did the same, a whole crowd of specks trembling and wandering in the drop, like sparks above a fire.
Brown watched us for a long time. I could see his great eye, enormous and brown, swimming above the lens.
'You are alive,' he whispered. 'That's it, isn't it? You are the living part of the pollen. You are trying to swim.'
It was a good guess. It was wrong. But Robert Brown was the kind of person who tests his good guesses, which is rarer than having them.
So he took pollen from plants that had been dried and pressed in his collection for many years. Surely that was dead. He crushed it into water. The specks danced.

He scraped dust from a piece of coal. It danced. He ground up glass, and the glass dust danced. He crushed bits of rock: granite, flint, even, he wrote later, a fragment of an old stone statue from Egypt. Every speck that was small enough danced in the water exactly as I did.

'It isn't life,' he said at last, sitting back, rubbing his eyes. 'Glass is not alive. Stone is not alive. Something is moving them. But what?' He looked at the drop for a long time. 'There's nothing there,' he said. 'Only water.'

He wrote it all down, carefully, and published it in 1828. He did not explain it. He could not. People read his paper and argued. Some said it was tiny currents in the water, some said it was heat, some said it was light from the lamp. Brown tested those ideas too, as well as he could, and the dance went on. He died in 1858, and the dance was still a mystery.
But I knew. I had known from the first moment. I just had no way to tell him.
What was moving me was the water.

Not the water as Robert Brown saw it, smooth and clear and still. The water as it really is: a crowd of particles so small that even his best lens could never show them, millions upon millions upon millions of them, each one far smaller than me, all of them rushing about, never resting, crashing into each other and into me from every side, more times every second than anyone could count.

When more of them happened to hit my left side than my right, I was shoved to the right. When more hit me from below, I was pushed up. It was like being a ball in the middle of a crowd of invisible children, all running about in a field, bumping into you without meaning to. I was not moving myself. The water was pushing me.

Seventy-eight years after that June morning, in 1905, a young man working in a patent office in Switzerland sat down with a pencil and worked it out. His name was Albert Einstein. He said: if the water is really made of moving molecules, then a speck like me should wander in just this way, and you can calculate how far. Three years later, in Paris, Jean Perrin watched specks like me through a better microscope, measured our zigzags, and found the numbers matched.
And so, because of a dance that no one could see the reason for, the world finally believed in atoms.

I like to think of that. Everything in Robert Brown's room was dancing too, though he never knew it: the glass, the brass of the microscope, the water in his teacup, the air he breathed out onto the lens, the particles of his own hand turning the screw. Nothing was still. Nothing has ever been still.
Only the dance was too small to see, until a speck from a pink flower showed it.
story.epiphany: Everything is made of particles that never stop moving. The jiggling of tiny specks (Brownian motion) is not life but the result of invisible water particles hitting them unevenly from all sides, and this became the evidence that atoms are real. The turn is the speck's 'I was not moving myself. The water was pushing me.' Based on Robert Brown's real 1827 observations (he did test old dried pollen, glass, coal and rock, and wrote of a fragment of the Sphinx). The speck's voice is imagined.
ask: What did Robert Brown first think made the specks move? How did he test it?
Why did the glass and stone dust prove the dancing wasn't life?
What was really moving the speck?
How did Einstein and Perrin finish what Brown started?
Is anything in this room perfectly still right now?

ideas.idea: Everything is made of particles that never stop moving.
ideas.more: In solids they vibrate in place, in liquids they slide past each other, in gases they race about. Heat is particles moving faster. Diffusion and Brownian motion are the evidence.

ideas.idea: Solid things are almost entirely empty space.
ideas.more: If an atom were as big as a stadium, its nucleus would be a pea in the middle. What feels solid is electric pushing between electrons.

ideas.idea: The same atoms cycle through everything.
ideas.more: The carbon in your body was made in stars long ago, and has been in rocks, air, plants and animals. The oxygen you breathe was split from water by plants. After you, your atoms will go on into other things.

ideas.idea: We can know about things too small to see, by their effects.
ideas.more: Nobody saw atoms for over 2,000 years after Kanada and Democritus imagined them. They were proved real by what they do: jiggle specks, spread colour, bounce particles back from foil. That is how science sees the invisible.

unknowns: What are particles really? Physicists describe them as ripples in invisible fields that fill space, but what those fields are, and whether there is something deeper still, nobody knows.

What is most of the universe made of? Scientists measure that ordinary matter, all the atoms in stars, planets and us, is only about a sixth of all the matter there is. The rest, called dark matter, has never been seen directly, and nobody yet knows what it is.

Why is there any matter at all? The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which destroy each other. Somehow a tiny bit more matter survived, and that is why we exist. Why, is still an open question.

check.q: What is matter? Is air matter? Is light?
check.a: Anything with mass that takes up space. Air is matter (it has mass, as the balloon balance showed). Light is not matter; it is energy.

check.q: Describe the particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas.
check.a: Solid: close, in rows, vibrating in place. Liquid: close but jumbled, sliding past each other. Gas: far apart, moving fast in all directions.

check.q: What is diffusion, and why is it faster in hot water?
check.a: Particles spreading from where there are many to where there are few. Hot particles move faster, so they spread faster.

check.q: What did Robert Brown see, and what did it prove?
check.a: Tiny specks jiggling in water. Einstein and Perrin showed it was caused by invisible water molecules hitting them, which proved atoms are real.

check.q: Why does a heavy wooden belan float while a small coin sinks?
check.a: Floating depends on density, not mass. Wood is less dense than water. The coin's metal is denser than water.

check.q: What did the gold foil experiment show about atoms?
check.a: Atoms are mostly empty space with a tiny, heavy nucleus in the centre.
Thinkers in ancient India and Greece who each taught that matter is made of tiny particles (paramanu, atomos), long before experiments proved atoms exist.
An Indian physicist who, with D.M. Bose, recorded tracks of particles from cosmic rays near Darjeeling in the early 1940s; her work was later overlooked.
